section.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets
section.sectionRationale: The eagle's cry at the end of chapter 8 announced three woes still to come, and this chapter delivers the first two of them in full. The fifth trumpet unleashes tormenting locust-scorpions from the Abyss under a king named Destruction, and the sixth releases four bound angels and a monstrous cavalry of two hundred million that kills a third of mankind, closing on the sobering note that survivors still refuse to repent. The chapter forms one complete unit, the first and second woes, before the interlude of chapter 10 delays the third woe and the seventh trumpet.
section.thesis: The first woe unleashes locust-scorpions from the Abyss, ruled by a king named Destruction in both Hebrew and Greek, to torment for five months everyone without God's seal, and the second woe releases a two hundred million strong cavalry that kills a third of mankind, yet even this does not move the survivors to repent of their idols, their murders, their sorceries, or their sexual immorality.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the star given the key to the Abyss and the smoke that darkens the sky; the locust-scorpions and their king, Abaddon and Apollyon; the sixth trumpet releasing the four angels and the two hundred million troops at the Euphrates; and mankind's continued, hardened refusal to repent.

verses.text: Then the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, and I saw a star that had fallen from heaven to earth, and it was given the key to the pit of the {{abyssos|Abyss}}.
The star opened the pit of the Abyss, and smoke rose out of it like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the pit.
And out of the smoke, locusts descended on the earth, and they were given power like that of the scorpions of the earth.
They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any plant or tree, but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
The locusts were not given power to kill them, but only to {{basanizo|torment}} them for five months, and their torment was like the stinging of a scorpion.
In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, but death will escape them.
And the locusts looked like horses prepared for battle, with something like crowns of gold on their heads, and faces like the faces of men.
They had hair like that of women, and teeth like those of lions.
They also had thoraxes like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the roar of many horses and chariots rushing into battle.
They had tails with stingers like scorpions, which had the power to injure people for five months.
They were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is {{apollyon|Apollyon}}.
The first woe has passed. Behold, two woes are still to follow.
Then the sixth angel sounded his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God
saying to the sixth angel with the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”
So the four angels who had been prepared for this hour and day and month and year were released to kill a third of mankind.
And the number of mounted troops was two hundred million; I heard their number.

Now the horses and riders in my vision looked like this: The riders had breastplates the colors of fire, sapphire, and sulfur. The heads of the horses were like the heads of lions, and out of their mouths proceeded fire, smoke, and sulfur.
A third of mankind was killed by the three plagues of fire, smoke, and sulfur that proceeded from their mouths.
For the power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails; indeed, their tails were like snakes, having heads with which to inflict harm.

Now the rest of mankind who were not killed by these plagues still did not {{metanoeo|repent}} of the works of their hands. They did not stop worshiping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk.
Furthermore, they did not repent of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft.

abyssos.gloss: The Abyss, the bottomless pit, the place of confinement for certain demonic beings, mentioned also in Luke 8:31 where demons beg not to be sent there. The star given its key pictures divine permission granted for a set and limited purpose, not a loss of God's control over what emerges from it.

basanizo.gloss: To torment, to test through pain, the same word used elsewhere in Revelation for the torment of the beast's followers. The locusts are explicitly denied the power to kill, only to torment for a limited five months, a severe but bounded affliction that leaves room for the tormented to still turn to God.

apollyon.gloss: Destroyer, the Greek name given for the king of the locust-Abyss, paired with its Hebrew equivalent Abaddon, Destruction. Both names describe not a creature to be admired or feared for its own sake, but the ruin and devastation that follow when God's restraining hand lifts to allow judgment on the unrepentant.

metanoeo.gloss: To repent, to change one's mind and direction fundamentally. Twice in this chapter's closing verses the survivors of catastrophic judgment are said to withhold this response, showing that the deepest tragedy of these plagues is not the suffering they cause but the hardened hearts that refuse to turn back to God even through them.

basic.context: The fifth trumpet releases smoke from the Abyss and out of it locust-scorpions that torment, but do not kill, everyone lacking God's seal, for five months of suffering so severe that people will long to die but cannot. These locusts are led by a king whose name means Destruction in both Hebrew and Greek. The sixth trumpet then releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, commanding a monstrous cavalry of two hundred million that kills a third of mankind with fire, smoke, and sulfur. The chapter ends on a sobering note: even after this much death, the survivors still refuse to repent of their idolatry or their moral corruption.
basic.hermeneutics: This is vivid, frightening imagery, and people rightly disagree about how literally to read the locusts, the two hundred million troops, and the timing of these events, whether tied to the fall of Jerusalem, patterns across church history, a still future tribulation, or timeless symbols of demonic assault on a rebellious world. What every faithful reading agrees on is this: even these terrifying judgments remain measured by God, sealed believers are protected from the locusts, and the tragedy is not merely the suffering inflicted but humanity's hardened refusal to turn back to God even under it.
basic.originalLanguages: The locusts emerge from the abyssos, the Abyss, the same bottomless pit demons beg not to be sent to elsewhere in the Gospels, opened here only by a key God permits to be used. Their assignment is only to basanizo, torment, not to kill, for a bounded five months. Their king bears the name apollyon, Destroyer, paired with the Hebrew Abaddon, both meaning ruin rather than describing an admirable power. And twice the chapter records that survivors did not metanoeo, repent, change their minds and turn back to God, even after catastrophic loss of life.
basic.typology: The locust plague recalls the eighth plague on Egypt in Exodus and Joel's terrifying locust army pictured as an invading force in the Day of the LORD. The army from the Euphrates recalls Israel's ancient invaders, Assyria and Babylon, who came from the east to execute God's judgment on an unfaithful people. And the Abyss itself anticipates its final use in Revelation 20, where the ancient serpent is bound there before his final judgment.
basic.christ: Christ is not directly pictured acting within this chapter, yet He is the one who already declared in Revelation 1:18 that He holds the keys of Death and Hades, meaning even the Abyss and its terrors operate only within limits He sets. The sealed servants of God, marked in chapter 7 by the Lamb's blood, are explicitly protected from the locusts' torment, showing that being found in Christ, not personal strength, is what shelters believers through this chapter's horrors.
basic.god: God permits terrifying judgment, yet even here His sovereignty measures and limits it: the locusts may torment but not kill, they may afflict only the unsealed, and their reign lasts a set five months. God is also patient even in severe judgment, since these plagues are meant to press hard enough to provoke repentance, yet He does not force it, and the chapter's saddest note is not what God does but what hardened human hearts refuse to do in response.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 10:12-15 describes the locust plague devastating Egypt, the background image behind this chapter's locusts. Joel 1:6-2:11 pictures a terrifying locust army as a sign of the coming Day of the LORD. Luke 8:31 shows demons begging Jesus not to send them into the Abyss, confirming His authority over that same place. Revelation 1:18 already declares that Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades.
basic.oneStory: From Egypt's locust plague to Joel's army of the Day of the LORD, the Bible has long pictured devastating judgment on a rebellious world using exactly this kind of vivid, terrifying imagery, and has always paired it with the tragic pattern of hardened hearts refusing to repent even under severe affliction. This chapter carries that whole story forward, showing that even the Abyss and its demonic locusts operate only within the bounds Christ Himself sets, that God's own sealed people are kept safe through it, and that the deepest tragedy in any generation is not suffering itself but a heart that will not turn back to God.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a matched pair of woes with a single sentence of sorrow between them, 'The first woe has passed. Behold, two woes are still to follow', verse 12. Each woe has the same structure: an angel sounds, something is released from a boundary, a force is described by a catalogue of comparisons, a limit is stated, and a name or number is given. For the locusts the boundary is the pit of the Abyss, for the cavalry it is the river Euphrates. The structure leads the reader to hear one pattern twice and to feel how the second is larger than the first.

The language of the chapter is the language of simile. John writes 'like' and 'something like' over and over. The locusts are 'like horses prepared for battle', with 'something like crowns of gold', faces 'like the faces of men', hair 'like that of women', teeth 'like those of lions', wings 'like the roar of many horses and chariots'. John is straining to describe what he saw and does not say that the creatures are these things. The riders in the sixth trumpet have breastplates 'the colors of fire, sapphire, and sulfur', and the horses have heads 'like the heads of lions'. A reader should hear the stammer in the style as part of its meaning, since the author is describing what does not fit ordinary categories.

Both woes are controlled by the passive voice. The star 'was given' the key, the locusts 'were given' power and 'were told' what not to harm, the four angels 'had been prepared' for the hour. Every limit is stated: the grass is spared, the sealed are spared, the torment lasts five months and does not kill. The sixth trumpet is bounded to a third.

The chapter ends on a note that is not a vision but a verdict. Verses 20 and 21 step out of the imagery and tell us what the survivors did, and it is the most sombre sentence of the chapter. The whole scene is arranged so that the final observation about hard hearts lands with force. Chapter 10 then interrupts, delaying the third woe, just as chapter 7 interrupted the seals.
context.historical:
Locusts were a feared reality in the ancient Near East. A swarm could strip a whole region of its crops in a day, and the plague of Egypt, Exodus 10:12 to 15, and the invasion described in Joel 1 and 2 were part of Israel's memory. Joel compares the swarm to an army: 'Their appearance is like that of horses, and they gallop like swift steeds', Joel 2:4. John takes this prophetic comparison and runs it in reverse, so that the insects of the prophets become something larger than insects, with an army's discipline and a scorpion's sting.

The Abyss was a place in the Jewish and early Christian imagination where unclean spirits and rebel powers were held. In the Gospels the demons begged Jesus not to order them into it, Luke 8:31, and the word occurs in Revelation for the origin of the beast, Revelation 11:7 and 17:8, and for the place where the dragon is bound, Revelation 20:1 to 3. A first reader would hear that the pit was a prison with a lid, and that the lid had now been lifted.

The Euphrates was the great boundary of the biblical world. It marked the northeastern edge of the land promised to Abraham, Genesis 15:18, and beyond it lay the powers from which Israel's worst invasions came. Assyria is called the razor hired from beyond the Euphrates, Isaiah 7:20, and later Babylon did the same. In John's day, the Parthian empire lay across the river, and Rome feared its mounted archers. The sixth trumpet's cavalry gathers these memories into a single picture.

Idolatry was part of the life of every city to which John wrote. The silver, gold, bronze, stone and wood in verse 20 are the materials of the statues that filled the temples, the markets and the emperor's shrines. The list of sins in verse 21 is the list of the pagan world as a Jewish or Christian reader would see it: bloodshed, magic, sexual license and theft. The people John addressed knew that the pressure to share in this world's worship was the very thing that separated them from their neighbours.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws more on Joel than on any other book. The day of the LORD in Joel is announced by a trumpet, Joel 2:1, and described as a locust army that comes as 'a day of darkness and gloom', Joel 2:2. Joel pictures an army 'like horses', Joel 2:4 and 5, and the same imagery returns in Revelation 9:7 to 9. Exodus supplies the earlier plague, in which the locusts covered the land and consumed everything green, Exodus 10:12 to 15, and Revelation reverses that detail by telling these locusts not to harm any plant.

The Abyss and its king have their own thread. In Job 26:6 and Proverbs 15:11 'Abaddon' is paired with Sheol as the place of destruction, laid open before God. John uses it as a title for the angel of the pit, so that a word for the place of the dead becomes the name of its ruler. The Abyss returns in Revelation 11:7, where the beast rises from it, in 17:8, and in 20:1 to 3 where an angel with a key and a chain throws the dragon into it and seals it over him. The star who receives the key in chapter 9 is balanced by the angel who receives it in chapter 20.

The Euphrates returns in Revelation 16:12, where the sixth bowl dries it up to prepare the way for the kings of the East. The sixth trumpet and the sixth bowl are matched.

The final verses belong to the Bible's long argument against idols. Psalm 115:4 to 7 says that idols have mouths but cannot speak, eyes but cannot see, and Daniel 5:23 speaks of gods 'which cannot see or hear or understand'. John joins the lists. The refusal to repent will be repeated in Revelation 16:9 and 16:11, where men curse God and do not give Him glory. Paul's reading of the human race in Romans 1 to 2 is the same: Romans 2:4 and 5 speaks of a hard and unrepentant heart which stores up wrath, while God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John writes so that the churches will not be shocked into thinking that the evil of their age is out of God's hands. The first woe has an exact limit, five months, and the cavalry of the second woe is bound by a boundary and a third. The reader who is tempted to ask whether God has lost the world is shown that the keys, the commands and the hours are all in His keeping.

He also writes to warn. This is the one chapter in the book where the narrator stops and observes what the judgments failed to do. The tone changes from description to diagnosis. The hearer is meant to take away the knowledge that suffering does not of itself produce repentance, and that the same hardness can sit in the heart of a person who has seen terrible things. A congregation that was tempted to think that if only the world could be shown the consequences of its sin it would turn, is told that this is not guaranteed.

And he writes for the sealed. Verse 4 states that the locusts may harm only those who lack the seal of God on their foreheads, so the chapter that is most frightening in its images is also a chapter of promise to those whom chapter 7 sealed. The church is not asked to fear the Abyss. It is asked to know that its Lord has the key, and that He has set the boundary. The chapter ends on the persistence of idolatry, which gives the church a reason to stay faithful: the pagan world is not simply a victim but a company of people who choose their gods.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter does not command anything. It describes what John saw and what people did, and the way to misread it is to turn it into a puzzle for decoding current affairs. Attempts to match the locusts to a particular weapon, or to compute the two hundred million into a particular army, claim more precision than the text supplies. John himself says 'like' repeatedly, and a vision built on similes does not invite a literal one to one decoding.

What is prescriptive, by implication, is the contrast between the world's response and the response God wants. The survivors 'did not repent' of their works, and the verb is given as a failure. The implied call is to do the opposite: to turn from idols, violence, sorcery, immorality and theft, and to turn to the living God. John sets the sins of the chapter against the hearers' own lives, because the same cities that produced the idols in verse 20 were the cities in which the churches lived.

The chapter also says something about how to hold fear. The images are meant to be terrifying, and the believer is not asked to feel less than that. Yet the sealed are protected, and the proper response is sober trust, not panic. A reader should also be wary of using this chapter to point at a group of people as the object of the woes. The people addressed by the woes are 'those who dwell on the earth', and the call to repent is open to anyone who hears it.

debates.question: Who is the fallen star with the key to the Abyss?

views.label: A good angel acting for God
views.case: Revelation 20:1 shows an angel coming down from heaven with the key to the Abyss, so a heavenly messenger with a key is a pattern in the book. The star is 'given' the key, which means God lends the authority, and stars stand for angels in Revelation 1:20. On this reading the 'fallen' star is simply one who has come down from heaven, sent to open the pit as God's instrument of judgment.

views.label: Satan or a demonic being
views.case: The star is 'fallen from heaven to earth', the language of a rebel. Isaiah 14:12 speaks of the day star who fell, and Revelation 12:9 says the dragon was hurled to the earth. The one who opens the pit and releases what comes from it is then the leader of what is released, and the locusts' king is 'the angel of the Abyss', verse 11. Some see the star and the king as the same figure.

debates.bearing: The first view sees a chain of authority that ends with God, and the second sees a stronger link between the star and the locusts. The text says the star was given the key, and that fact holds either way: whoever opens the Abyss does so under God's permission, and the chapter's concern is with the limits, not the identity.

debates.question: Is the cavalry of the sixth trumpet human or demonic?

views.label: A human army
views.case: The Euphrates was the frontier from which invading armies came, and 'mounted troops' with breastplates is language of the battlefield. Many see an eastern invasion, whether a past one such as the Parthians or a future one. The killing of a third of mankind by fire, smoke and sulfur is then literal warfare, and the verb 'kill' is used straightforwardly.

views.label: A demonic host
views.case: The four angels are bound, and in Scripture bound angels are rebellious spirits, as with the Abyss in the fifth trumpet. The horses have lion's heads and snake tails, which is not how ordinary soldiers are described. The parallel with the locusts, which are certainly not natural, suggests that the cavalry is the same order of being. The number is also enormous, and the images are those of the unseen powers.

debates.bearing: The text blends the two: its imagery is military and its creatures are monstrous. A reader does not have to settle the question to see the main point, that the powers released are on a leash, that a third is the limit, and that none of it moves the survivors. The theological weight rests on the last two verses, not on identifying the riders.

study.originalLanguages:
The Abyss is abyssos, literally 'bottomless', from a, 'without', and byssos, 'depth'. The word in the Greek Old Testament is used for the deep of the sea, as in Genesis 1:2, and the New Testament narrows it to a place of confinement for spirits, as in Luke 8:31. John calls the opening in verse 1 a 'pit', phrear, a well or shaft, and the picture is of a deep shaft with a lid. The star 'was given' the key, edothe, the divine passive again. John says the star had fallen, using a perfect participle, which means it is in the state of having fallen: the fall is past and its result remains.

In verse 5 the torment is basanismos, the noun for torture or tormenting, with the verb basanizo behind it. The locusts are not allowed to kill, only to torment, and the long wish for death in verse 6 is the result. The verse uses a pair of verbs for seeking and not finding, and for desiring to die while death 'flees'. John's phrase says that death, which in chapter 6 rode out, now escapes, and the pair has a bitter irony.

The locusts are akrides, and their power is compared to scorpions, skorpioi. The time limit 'five months' is a sentence John gives twice, in verses 5 and 10,. The long catalogue of comparisons in verses 7 to 10 is built with 'like' or 'as', homoios and hos, a sign that John is describing resemblance.

The king's name is given in two languages: in Hebrew Abaddon, in Greek Apollyon. Abaddon comes from the Hebrew root for perishing or being destroyed, and it appears in Job 26:6 and Proverbs 15:11 as a name for the place of destruction. Apollyon is a participle meaning 'the Destroyer', a present participle of the Greek verb for destroy or perish. John gives the name in two languages so that Jew and Gentile alike would hear it, and the effect is of a title that needs no translation.

In verse 15 the four angels 'had been prepared for this hour and day and month and year'. The Greek has one article before the four time words, which most commentators read as a single appointed moment named with increasing precision, though some take it as a span of time. In either reading, the point is that the timing was fixed before it came.

The number 'two hundred million' is dismyriades myriadon, 'two myriads of myriads', a myriad being ten thousand. John says 'I heard their number', as he did for the sealed in chapter 7, so that this is a number that has been told and not counted.

The verbs of the last two verses matter most. 'Repent' is metanoeo, to change one's mind and direction, and it is used negatively twice: they did not repent of the works of their hands and they did not repent of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality and theft. The word for sorcery is pharmakeia, from which we get 'pharmacy', which covers the use of drugs in magic. The word for 'demons' is daimonia, and John says that their worship of idols is, in truth, worship of demons, the same claim made in Deuteronomy 32:17 and 1 Corinthians 10:20.

typology.type: The locust plague, Exodus 10:12 to 15 and Joel 1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: In Egypt locusts came on an east wind and ate everything green, and in Joel they were an army sent by the LORD's command at the day of the LORD. The fifth trumpet's locusts keep the army and the darkness, but reverse the target: they spare the grass and the trees and attack people. The correspondence is that creatures do the LORD's bidding as His army. The escalation is that these torment people directly and come from the Abyss, so that the plague is no longer of nature but of the spiritual realm. The type falls short in that the earlier plagues stripped the harvest, while these strike the persons who refuse the seal, and they cannot kill.

typology.type: The Euphrates frontier, Genesis 15:18 and Isaiah 7:20
typology.fulfillment: The great river marked the boundary of the promised land, and beyond it lay the powers that invaded Israel as God's rod of discipline. Isaiah called Assyria a razor hired from beyond the Euphrates. The sixth trumpet's cavalry comes from that edge, held back until the appointed hour. The correspondence is of invasion from beyond the border as God's judgment on a people who forgot Him. The escalation is that the river now bounds the world's whole rebellion, and the army is released against the nations themselves and not just against Israel. The type falls short because the earlier invaders were nations with names, and these are unnamed and numberless.

When the plague eased, Pharaoh hardened his heart and refused to listen, and the pattern repeated through the plagues. The survivors of the sixth trumpet did the same, and still did not repent. The correspondence is that signs of judgment, however severe, do not by themselves turn a resistant heart. The escalation is that Revelation widens the pattern from one king to the whole world's inhabitants, and Revelation 16:9 and 16:11 repeat it. The type falls short in the one respect that Nineveh offers: when Jonah warned the city, the people turned from their evil ways and God relented, Jonah 3:8 to 10. So judgment can bring repentance, and repentance can still be had.

typology.type: The key of the Abyss, Revelation 20:1 to 3
typology.fulfillment: The star is given the key and opens the pit, and in chapter 20 an angel holds the same key and locks the dragon in. The pit that releases the locusts becomes the cell that holds the serpent. The correspondence is of the Abyss under a divine key. The escalation is that what is opened for a limited time in chapter 9 is shut and sealed for good in chapter 20. Christ declares that He holds the keys of Death and Hades, Revelation 1:18, which is the ground of both. The type falls short only in that the full closing of the pit lies ahead, and chapter 9 shows only the opening.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ by the key. The star receives it by gift, and the Lord of the book has already said, 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades', Revelation 1:18. The locusts' king is the angel of the Abyss, but his kingdom is a loan. Satan's power over those who dwell on the earth is real, but it cannot reach beyond the command given. That one phrase is the answer to the dread of the chapter: whatever comes up from the pit does so because the one who was dead and is alive has let it, and He will shut it again.

It points to Christ by the seal. The locusts may harm only 'those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads'. The seal is the name of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 14:1, and it is given through the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 7:14. The protection offered here is not a reward for good behaviour but the result of belonging to Him. Paul says that those who are in Christ have been sealed with the Spirit, Ephesians 1:13 and 14, and Jesus said that no one can snatch His sheep from His hand, John 10:28. The torment that others endure is the torment from which His people are shielded.

It points to Christ by contrast with the survivors. They would not give up the idols that 'cannot see or hear or walk', and the Gospel says that Jesus came to give sight, to make the deaf hear and the lame walk, Matthew 11:5. The idols are dead things and the Lamb is the Living One. The comparison is a reminder of what the world gives up when it refuses Him.

And it points to Christ in the last two verses, by what is left unsaid. The one who died for sinners offers repentance freely, and the New Testament names this as the purpose of His patience, 2 Peter 3:9, and of His kindness, Romans 2:4. The chapter ends with the failure to repent, and so it leaves a space that only He can fill. The call that Jesus began His ministry with, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near', Matthew 4:17, is the call that these survivors do not answer. We should not read each detail of the locusts as a picture of Christ. The chapter points to Him through the key He holds, the seal He gives and the repentance He offers, and the grotesque images are not to be given a christological meaning of their own.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the one who sets the boundary. The Abyss is opened only by a given key. The locusts are told what not to harm, and for how long. The angels at the Euphrates are bound until the hour. Every threat is held in a fist, and the writer lets us see the fingers. This is perhaps the strongest teaching on God's sovereignty in the chapter: the powers of darkness exist and act, but never beyond the limit of the permission they are given. The doctrine does not make God the author of evil, and the chapter keeps the difference in view. The star and the locusts and the angels do what they will, and God sets the edges of what they may do. It is what Job learned, Job 1:12 and 2:6, and what Paul says of the temptations we face, that God will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, 1 Corinthians 10:13.

He is the God who discriminates. The sealed are spared, while others suffer. This is not favouritism, since the seal is available to all through the Lamb, but it is a sign that God knows His own and that His protection is real and specific. The Lord who sealed His servants in chapter 7 acts on that sealing here.

He is a God who judges the idolatry that dishonours Him. The final verses say what the judgments are about. People are making gods of silver and gold that cannot see or hear, and doing violence, sorcery, immorality and theft. In God's judgment the worship of what is not God and the harm done to what He made are bound together: the first table of the law and the second fall in the same sentence. Isaiah's contempt for the maker of idols, Isaiah 44:9 and 10, comes to its end in a world in which the idols are demons and the people who serve them are broken by them.

He is also the God who is patient, and the chapter shows how patience is spent. Five months of torment that does not kill, a third and not all, and warnings given again and again leave time and space for turning. When the survivors do not repent, the patient God is not shown to be weak. He is shown to be just in what follows. Paul says that anyone who disregards the riches of God's kindness is storing up wrath, Romans 2:4 and 5.

For worship this means that we praise a God whose limits are as holy as His power. We trust Him with the pit and the river, because He holds both. We also take the last verse as an examination of our own hearts: the right response to His works is to turn, and a worship that never turns from the idols of the age is not what He asked for.

crossReferences.note: The prophet blows the trumpet for the day of the LORD and pictures an army of locusts whose appearance is like horses and whose sound is like chariots. John's locusts take over these comparisons in verses 7 to 9, which marks them as the day of the LORD's army.

Locusts swarmed over Egypt from an east wind and ate everything green that the hail had left. The fifth trumpet recalls this plague and reverses its target, since these locusts are told to spare the plants and attack people without the seal.

The demons begged Jesus not to order them into the Abyss. The word shows that it was known as a place of confinement for spirits, so the fifth trumpet's opening of the pit means that powers normally shut up are released for a time.

Sheol is naked before God and Abaddon has no covering. This is where the name Abaddon comes from, and it shows that even the place of destruction is open before God, so the king of the Abyss rules a realm that remains under His sight.

An angel comes down with the key to the Abyss and a great chain, seizes the dragon and shuts and seals the pit over him. The key given in chapter 9 for a limited release is balanced by this final locking, which shows that the Abyss is always under a hand.

God gave Abram the land to the great River Euphrates. The river that marks the edge of the promised land is the boundary from which the sixth trumpet's armies come, which fits the way Israel's invaders came from across it.

The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings of the East. The sixth trumpet and sixth bowl are matched at the same river, which suggests that the series return to the same scene with growing weight.

The idols of the nations are silver and gold, with mouths that cannot speak and feet that cannot walk. Verse 20 draws on this long mockery of idols, and the psalm explains why the survivors' worship is empty as well as wrong.

Israel sacrificed to demons and not to God. John's claim that those who worship idols are worshiping demons has its root here, and Paul uses the same teaching in 1 Corinthians 10:20 when he says that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons.

Nineveh turned from its evil ways when warned, and God relented. This is the answer to Revelation 9:20 and 21, since it shows that judgment can bring repentance and that God is ready to respond when people turn.

God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance, and a hard and unrepentant heart stores up wrath. Paul describes in general what John shows in particular: the survivors who will not repent are the ones who despise the riches of God's patience.

study.oneStory:
The first plague of the Bible's great deliverance, Exodus, ended in a hard heart, and the story told here ends the same way. From Pharaoh to the survivors of the sixth trumpet, the Bible keeps asking whether a sign of God's power will bring a person to turn, and keeps answering that signs alone do not. This is the old problem of Genesis 3 in its later form. The first man and woman had been given every tree and one command, and they believed the serpent over God. Now their descendants have seen the Lord strike the world and still reach for the work of their own hands.

The chapter also tells the story of the serpent's career. The pit, the locusts and their king are an unveiling of what has been behind the human drama from the beginning. The serpent of Genesis 3 is named by Revelation 12:9, and in this chapter his order is released on those who bear no seal. The story of creation, fall and redemption has an enemy, and the enemy is allowed a measure of rope so that all can see what he does with it.

It tells, too, of how God's people are kept. Israel in Egypt was shielded from the plagues that struck the land, Exodus 8:22 and 10:23, and the sealed here are shielded from the locusts. The story of the exodus is rerun on the largest scale: a people marked, a power that will not let go, plagues that fall on the unmarked, and a rescue still to come. The sealed are in the world but not hurt by what hurts it.

And it moves the story toward its end. The two woes build to the third, and the third is the seventh trumpet, which announces the kingdom of the world as the kingdom of Christ, Revelation 11:15. The Abyss that was opened by a given key is locked and sealed in chapter 20, and the river that bounded the promised land will in the end be crossed by the river of the water of life, Revelation 22:1. The story ends in a place where there is no more curse, nothing from the pit, and nothing to torment, because all that was in the Abyss has been shut in and the idols have been taken away. The chapter shows the story at its hardest, and by naming the hard heart as the real tragedy it makes room for the grace of the one who calls even now to repent.

sermon.title: Revelation (Part 13): Revelation 8-10
sermon.why: Carson works through Revelation 8 through 10 verse by verse in this message, including direct exposition of the fifth and sixth trumpets, the locusts, and mankind's continued refusal to repent in 9:20-21, engaging the specific content of this section within its wider structural context.

quiz.q: What are the locusts of the fifth trumpet given power to do, and to whom?

options.text: To torment, but not kill, for five months, only those without the seal of God on their foreheads.
options.note: Verses 4-5 specify exactly this limited scope and target of the locusts' power.

options.text: To kill everyone on earth instantly.
options.note: The text explicitly denies the locusts power to kill; their assignment is torment, not death.

options.text: To destroy all the earth's vegetation.
options.note: Verse 4 explicitly commands the locusts not to harm the grass, plants, or trees, unlike ordinary locusts.

options.text: To harm only those already sealed by God.
options.note: The opposite is true; those sealed by God are explicitly protected from the locusts' torment.

quiz.q: What is the name of the king who rules the locusts, and what does it mean?

options.text: Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, both meaning Destruction or Destroyer.
options.note: Verse 11 gives both names and their shared meaning of ruin and destruction.

options.text: Michael, the archangel who leads God's armies.
options.note: Michael appears elsewhere in Scripture as an angel who fights for God's people; the king of the locusts here is named Abaddon and Apollyon, not Michael.

options.text: Beelzebul, a name used for Satan in the Gospels.
options.note: That name appears in the Gospels for the ruler of demons, but this chapter specifically names the locusts' king Abaddon and Apollyon.

options.text: The text gives no name for the locusts' ruler.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly names him in both Hebrew and Greek.

quiz.q: What is released at the sounding of the sixth trumpet?

options.text: Four angels bound at the Euphrates, commanding two hundred million mounted troops who kill a third of mankind.
options.note: Verses 13-18 describe exactly this release and its devastating effect.

options.text: A single angel who immediately ends all judgment.
options.note: The sixth trumpet releases four angels and a massive army bringing further devastating judgment, not an ending of judgment.

options.text: The 144,000 sealed servants from chapter 7.
options.note: The 144,000 were sealed and protected in chapter 7; the sixth trumpet releases four bound angels and their army of judgment, an entirely different scene.

options.text: The seventh seal, completing the scroll's judgments.
options.note: The seventh seal was already opened in chapter 8; this chapter concerns the fifth and sixth trumpets, not the seals.

quiz.q: What is the source of the three plagues that kill a third of mankind in the sixth trumpet?

options.text: Fire, smoke, and sulfur proceeding from the mouths of the horses in the vision.
options.note: Verses 17-18 describe exactly this source of the deadly plagues.

options.text: A famine caused by the black horse of the third seal.
options.note: That famine belongs to the earlier seal judgments in chapter 6, not the sixth trumpet's plagues of fire, smoke, and sulfur.

options.text: Locusts stinging with their tails like scorpions.
options.note: That description belongs to the fifth trumpet's locusts, not the sixth trumpet's cavalry, though both involve tails causing harm.

options.text: The text does not specify a source for the plagues.
options.note: Verses 17-18 explicitly identify fire, smoke, and sulfur from the horses' mouths as the source.

quiz.q: How do the survivors of these plagues respond, according to verses 20-21?

options.text: They still did not repent of their idolatry, murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, or theft.
options.note: Verses 20-21 record this exact and sobering refusal to repent.

options.text: They immediately turned to God in repentance and faith.
options.note: The text explicitly records the opposite: continued refusal to repent despite the severity of the judgment.

options.text: They repented of their idolatry but continued in their immorality.
options.note: The text names both their continued idolatry and their continued moral sins together; no partial repentance is described.

options.text: They were all destroyed, leaving no survivors to respond at all.
options.note: The text specifically addresses 'the rest of mankind who were not killed,' meaning survivors remained and their response is described.

questions: The locusts could torment but not kill, and only for a set time. Where have you experienced hardship that felt limitless but was, in fact, bounded by God's mercy and timing?
Those sealed by God were untouched by the locusts' torment. What does it mean to you, practically, that your security rests on belonging to Christ rather than on your own strength to endure hardship?

Even catastrophic judgment did not move the survivors to repent. Is there an area of your own life where you have grown so used to your idols or your sin that even hardship has not moved you to turn back to God?

The chapter names specific sins, idolatry, murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft, as what people would not repent of. Which of these, or their modern equivalents, do you find hardest to honestly name and confess in your own life?

Even the Abyss and its terrifying locusts operate only because Christ permits it, holding the keys of Death and Hades. How does trusting Christ's authority over every power, seen and unseen, change the way you face fear today?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote explains that Abaddon means Destruction in Hebrew, and Apollyon means Destroyer in Greek, John deliberately supplying both names so that both Jewish and Greek-speaking readers would grasp the ruin this figure represents.

The description that people 'will seek death and will not find it' is a striking reversal of the usual human fear of death, underscoring the severity of the locusts' torment as worse, in the sufferers' own estimation, than dying.

The list of unrepented sins pairs idolatry, worship of demons and lifeless idols, with moral corruption, murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft, reflecting a consistent biblical pattern where false worship and moral collapse are shown to be deeply intertwined.
